sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The Celts counted the crane among their symbolic animals. Both birds and trees, the Celts taught, reached into two worlds at once, here and in the Otherworld. A crane made its home in the air, on land, and in the water. That range made it magical. Cranes stood for the feminine power, often when seen as three. Cranes walk upright, so people thought they were human once. Folk belief links the crane to bad will and miserliness. In the story of the children of Lir, the cruel sorceress Aife changed Fionnuala and her brothers into swans. A curse then turned Aife herself into a crane. Cursing could use a crane-like pose, one leg raised and one arm stretched out. The goddess Badb took this pose at the hostel of Da Derga, laying a curse on Conaire for the vows he had broken. A taboo on eating the flesh of a crane is old. Some believe the bird was once an ancestral god or a symbol.

okr.objective: The crane is a magical symbolic animal in Celtic belief.
